findings.title: Issue-tracker API key returned in product API responses to any user with read (View) permission
findings.rationale: Root cause is `ProductCoreSerializer.to_representation` at backend/application/core/api/serializers_product.py:123. It serializes every model field (the base `Meta.fields = "__all__"`, inherited via `__all__`/`exclude` by the subclasses) and never masks `issue_tracker_api_key`. The fix pops `issue_tracker_api_key` from the output unless the caller holds `Permissions.Product_Edit`, reusing the `permissions` value the serializer already computes via `get_permissions`. It mirrors the existing precedent `ApiConfigurationSerializer.to_representation` (import_observations/api/serializers.py:111-119) that gates `api_key` on `Api_Configuration_Edit`. Placing it in the base `to_representation` fixes both serializers named in the finding (`ProductSerializer` and `ProductListSerializer`) at one inheritance point. The field stays writable (no `write_only`), so `validate()` at line 377 — which reads `attrs.get("issue_tracker_api_key")` from input — is unaffected; this only filters the *response* representation. `data.pop(..., None)` is null-safe for serializers that exclude the field.
findings.variants_checked: ProductCoreSerializer.to_representation (base, the fix site), ProductSerializer.Meta, ProductListSerializer.Meta — all three resolve to the single inherited `to_representation`. Also grepped every `issue_tracker_api_key` usage: core/models.py:101 (field def), serializers_product.py:385/390 (input validation, unaffected), and the three issue_tracker backends (gitlab/github/jira_issue_tracker.py) which read the field server-side, not via the API serializer. NestedProductSerializer/NestedProductListSerializer/NestedProductSerializerSmall do NOT inherit ProductCoreSerializer (they subclass ModelSerializer directly): the small/list nested ones use `fields`/`exclude` that omit issue tracker fields anyway; NestedProductSerializer (excludes only members/auth groups) is used as `product_data` inside ApiConfigurationSerializer/ProductMemberSerializer — these expose the product's full field set including the key, so they would need the same gate. Flagged below rather than silently expanding scope, since the finding scopes f001 to ProductSerializer/ProductListSerializer and NestedProductSerializer is a separate sink with its own permission context.
findings.bypass_considered: I tried reaching the key through the list endpoint (`ProductListSerializer`) since the finding flags it separately — but it inherits the same base `to_representation`, so the pop applies there too. I also considered a Reader spoofing the gate: the check reads `data["permissions"]`, which is produced server-side by `get_permissions(get_highest_user_role(obj))` from the requesting user's actual role, not from client input, so a Reader cannot inject `Product_Edit`. The one genuine residual path is `NestedProductSerializer` (e.g. embedded as `product_data` in API-configuration/member responses), which does not inherit this base and still emits the key — that is a distinct sink outside f001's stated scope and is called out in variants_checked for a follow-up finding rather than masked here, since over-broadening would change unrelated serializer contracts.
findings.test_note: Added `test_issue_tracker_api_key_hidden_without_edit` to backend/unittests/core/api/test_serializers.py in the existing `TestBranchSerializer` class (same class the sibling `test_get_permissions_user` lives in), following the established `@patch(... get_permissions_for_role / get_highest_user_role)` pattern. It asserts the key is absent for a Reader (Product_View only) and present for Product_Edit. Fails before the change (key always serialized), passes after.
findings.review_reason: The fix lands in `ProductCoreSerializer.to_representation` (diff line 7-10), the base-class method inherited by `ProductSerializer` at source line 272/295, so it is squarely on the call path from the LOCATION; `issue_tracker_api_key` (a credential CharField, models.py:101) is otherwise serialized to any View-permission user because line 295's exclude list omits it. It is a root-cause authorization gate keyed on the already-computed `Permissions.Product_Edit`, fails closed via `data.get("permissions") or []`, adds no new input parsing or weakened validation, and the only other inheritor (`ProductGroupSerializer`) excludes the field so the `pop(..., None)` is a safe no-op. The accompanying test hunk covers both the hidden and visible cases, and the change matches surrounding serializer style.

findings.title: Issue-tracker API key stored unencrypted while siblings use EncryptedCharField
findings.rationale:
Root cause: `backend/application/core/models.py:101` declared `issue_tracker_api_key` as a plain `CharField`, so the live issue-tracker credential (GitHub/GitLab Bearer token, Jira/GitLab basic-auth password) was written to the `core_product` DB column in cleartext, while every other integration secret in the codebase (`access_control/models.py:104` `JWT_Secret.secret`, `import_observations/models.py:44/49` `Api_Configuration.api_key`/`basic_auth_password`) uses `EncryptedCharField`. The fix changes the field to `EncryptedCharField`, matching the sibling pattern exactly (including the `# nosemgrep` / "treat as regular CharField" comment the project uses on its other encrypted fields), and imports the field the same way the sibling models do.

The schema change alone only protects future writes; existing rows stay plaintext. So the migration `0087` pairs the `AlterField` with a `RunPython` data migration that re-saves every non-empty row via `bulk_update`, forcing `EncryptedMixin.get_db_prep_save` to encrypt the stored value. This is safe because `EncryptedMixin.to_python` (fields.py:72-75) catches `InvalidToken` and returns the plaintext unchanged, so reading the not-yet-migrated rows during the migration yields the correct cleartext to re-encrypt. The migration follows the existing paginator/`bulk_update` style of `core/0073_initialize_default_branch.py` and the `AlterField`-to-`EncryptedCharField` shape of `import_observations/0005`. `reverse_code` is a noop, matching project convention (a reverse re-encrypt is impossible to express generically and the column type reverts via Django's automatic `AlterField` reversal).

`issue_tracker_username` was deliberately left as a plain `CharField`: it is an identity, not a credential, and the directly analogous sibling `Api_Configuration.basic_auth_username` (`import_observations/models.py:48`) is also a plain `CharField` while only the password is encrypted. Matching that precedent keeps the change minimal and consistent.
findings.variants_checked:
Grepped every consumer of the field to confirm no other storage site or alternate write path bypasses the model field:
- `issue_tracker/issue_trackers/github_issue_tracker.py:124` (reads `product.issue_tracker_api_key` into Bearer header) — read-only, decrypts transparently, unaffected.
- `issue_tracker/issue_trackers/gitlab_issue_tracker.py:119` (PRIVATE-TOKEN header) — read-only, unaffected.
- `issue_tracker/issue_trackers/jira_issue_tracker.py:21-22` (basic_auth username+key) — read-only; confirmed username is paired as Jira account id, not a secret.
- `core/api/serializers_product.py:385-407` (validation/write of `issue_tracker_api_key`/`issue_tracker_username`) — goes through the model field, so encryption is automatic; no raw SQL.
- Sibling encrypted fields `access_control/models.py:104` `JWT_Secret.secret`, `import_observations/models.py:44/49` `Api_Configuration.api_key`/`basic_auth_password` — already `EncryptedCharField`; my change brings the issue-tracker field in line with them.
No other model stores an issue-tracker token; the only persistence is this one field.
findings.bypass_considered: Variation tried: a token that is itself a syntactically valid Fernet token at write time (or an attacker who can pre-seed the column with valid-looking ciphertext) — would `to_python` mangle it and let a plaintext slip through on a later read? No: on write, `get_db_prep_save` unconditionally Fernet-encrypts whatever string is supplied, so even a Fernet-shaped input is double-wrapped and stored as ciphertext; the plaintext never reaches the column. The only path that returns a value verbatim is `to_python`'s `InvalidToken` fallback on read, which is a decrypt path, not a write path, and cannot cause cleartext to be persisted. The other conceivable bypass — a future code path writing the token via raw SQL — is out of scope here because no such path exists today (variant grep above), and would be a new vulnerability rather than a way around this field change. So no input variation reaches "credential stored in cleartext" after the field is encrypted.
findings.test_note: Added `backend/unittests/core/test_issue_tracker_api_key_encryption.py`. It creates a `Product` with a known token, confirms the ORM reads it back intact (decryption works), then reads the raw `core_product.issue_tracker_api_key` column via a DB cursor and asserts the plaintext token is absent. Before the change the raw column equals the plaintext (test fails on the `assertNotEqual`/`assertNotIn`); after the change the column holds Fernet ciphertext (test passes). The unittest environment supplies a working `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (`docker/backend/unittests/envs/django`), and the test extends the existing `unittests.base_test_case.BaseTestCase`, matching the project's test layout (`backend/unittests/core/`).
findings.review_reason: The diff converts the plaintext credential field at models.py:101 to `EncryptedCharField` (diff line 16), exactly mirroring the established repo pattern at `import_observations/models.py:44` and `access_control/models.py:104`, with the dependency already declared in `pyproject.toml`. It is a root-cause fix (encryption at rest), not suppression — the `# nosemgrep` matches existing convention, not a silencing of the real issue. The accompanying migration `0087` correctly chains from `0086` and re-encrypts existing plaintext rows via `RunPython`, and the added test asserts the raw column no longer contains the plaintext token; no new attack surface or weakened validation is introduced.

findings.title: Committed default DJANGO_SECRET_KEY in shipped prod compose
findings.rationale: Root cause is the committed literal default in the compose interpolation `${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:-<literal>}` at docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:85, not the Django sink. backend/config/settings/base.py:29 does `SECRET_KEY = env("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY")` with no Python fallback, so whatever compose resolves becomes the live key. If the operator never sets SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, the `:-` fallback supplies the world-readable committed key, which signs sessions and password-reset tokens — an attacker who knows it can forge them. The fix changes `:-` (substitute-if-unset) to `:?message` (Docker Compose error-if-unset-or-empty). This enforces that the operator must provide a per-deployment key; `docker compose up` aborts with the error message instead of silently booting with the known key. No secret value remains in the file. Note: the exposed key in git history still needs rotation operationally — that is out of scope for a code diff.
findings.variants_checked: Same literal `${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:-NxYPEF5l...}` pattern present in docker-compose-prod-mysql.yml:85 and docker-compose-prod-test.yml:52 (sibling shipped prod compose files — same bug, outside this finding's scoped file f006; should be fixed by the same one-line change there). docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:86 FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY has the identical committed-literal-default antipattern (encrypts stored fields) and warrants the same `:?` treatment, but it is a distinct secret and outside f006's scope, so I left it untouched and flag it here. charts/secobserve/values.yaml:165 uses `valueFrom: secretKeyRef` — no literal, not vulnerable. dev/unittest/playwright compose files keep literal defaults intentionally and are not prod surfaces.
findings.bypass_considered: Tried: operator exports `SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=` (empty string). With the old `:-` this would still trigger the fallback to the literal; the question is whether my change catches it. The `:?` form (as opposed to `-?`) errors on both unset AND empty, so an empty export also aborts the launch. The remaining residual is an operator who explicitly sets a weak/known value — compose cannot judge key quality, only presence; that is a documentation/entropy concern, not reachable through the interpolation-default path this fix closes.
findings.test_note: No test added. The project's test suite (backend/unittests/) is a Django/Python unittest suite with no harness that parses or validates docker-compose YAML env defaults. A regression test would require introducing a new YAML/grep or shell test category foreign to the repo's conventions, which exceeds the minimal-diff mandate. The change is also self-verifying at runtime: `docker compose -f docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml config` (or `up`) now exits non-zero with the error message when SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is unset, whereas before it silently substituted the committed key.
findings.review_reason: The single hunk at docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:85 replaces the hardcoded `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` fallback (`${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:-NxYP...}`) with the fail-closed `${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:?...}` form, removing the embedded secret at its root and forcing operators to supply one rather than suppressing the finding. No new parsing, trusted input, or weakened validation is introduced; failing startup when the var is unset is strictly more secure. It matches native Compose `${VAR:?}` style and is minimal; the only nit is that the adjacent `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` on line 86 (and the same pattern in prod-mysql.yml:85/prod-test.yml:52) carries the identical issue but is out of scope for this line-scoped finding.

findings.title: Committed default FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY defeats at-rest field encryption
findings.rationale:
Root cause is two-layered. The cited sink (docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:86) supplies a world-known Fernet key via the `${SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-DtlkqVb3...=}` fallback, so a no-op `docker compose up` runs with a public key. But the deeper root cause is `backend/config/settings/base.py:432`, which read `env("FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY")` with no validation — THREAT_MODEL.md:112 lists exactly this fail-closed boot check as a still-missing control, and many other files (helm chart, dev compose, CI scripts) also carry the same key.

Fix at both layers, smallest change each:
- Compose: swap `:-default` for `:?error` so an unset `SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` makes compose abort with a pointer to the key-generation docs, instead of silently substituting the burned key. No literal secret remains in the cited file.
- Code (the true root cause): `base.py:432` now routes the value through a new pure helper `validate_field_encryption_key`, which raises `ImproperlyConfigured` if the key is empty or equals any known-burned default. This enforces fail-closed regardless of which deployment path (compose, helm, manual env, .env) supplied the value, so it catches the variants the compose-only edit cannot. The helper lives in `application/commons/services/settings_validation.py` with zero Django-model imports so it is safe to import at settings-load time.
findings.variants_checked: Grepped `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` / `DtlkqVb3wlaVdJK` across the repo. Sibling injection sites carrying the same burned key: docker-compose-prod-mysql.yml:86, docker-compose-prod-test.yml:53, docker-compose-dev.yml:41, docker-compose-dev-mysql.yml:41, docker-compose-dev-keycloak.yml:50, docker-compose-playwright.yml:47, docker-compose-unittests.yml:20, docker/backend/unittests/envs/django:15, backend/bin/run_pylint.sh:19, backend/bin/run_mypy.sh:19, charts/secobserve/values.yaml:173. Consumer: config/settings/base.py:432 (single read point). I did not edit the dev/test/CI/unittest files or the helm chart: those are intentionally-static test fixtures or operator-supplied secret references, and the `base.py` fail-closed check now defends every production boot path centrally. The gitleaks parser fixtures and TRIAGE/VULN/THREAT_MODEL docs that mention the key are reporting artifacts, not config, and were left untouched.
findings.bypass_considered: Attacker variation: set `SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to the burned key explicitly (the compose `:?` only catches *unset*, not a deliberately-supplied bad value), or supply it via helm/`.env`/manual `-e`. The compose-only edit would not stop this. The `base.py` helper does: it checks the resolved value against `BURNED_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` and raises regardless of source, so every path that ends at `base.py:432` fails closed. Residual gap: a different but still public key not in the burned set would pass — addressed by documenting per-deployment key generation rather than enumerable blocklisting; entropy validation of an arbitrary key is out of scope for this finding.
findings.test_note: Added backend/unittests/commons/services/test_settings_validation.py (alongside the existing commons/services tests). It uses `django.test.SimpleTestCase` (no DB) since the helper is pure. `test_burned_default_key_rejected` and `test_empty_key_rejected` fail before the change (no helper / no validation) and pass after; `test_fresh_key_accepted` guards against over-blocking. A direct test of `base.py`'s module-level raise was avoided because the settings module imports at suite startup with the burned key still in the unittest env, which would break the whole run — hence the extracted, independently-testable helper.
findings.review_reason: The core approach is correct and root-cause (compose line 86 made mandatory via `:?`, and `base.py:432` now fail-closes through `validate_field_encryption_key`, matching the existing `raise ValueError` style at base.py:437-438), and it adds no new attack surface. But it is incomplete and regresses tests: `unittests.py`→`prod.py`→`base.py` runs the new burned-key check, while the test/CI environments still feed that exact key (`docker/backend/unittests/envs/django:15`, `docker-compose-unittests.yml:20`, `run_pylint.sh:19`, `run_mypy.sh:19`), so settings import will raise ImproperlyConfigured and break the suite, pylint, and mypy. It also only patches one of the shipped compose files — the identical default still lives in `docker-compose-prod-mysql.yml:86` and `docker-compose-prod-test.yml:53`, leaving the vulnerability active in sibling production artifacts.

findings.title: Stored XSS via SBOM component names assigned to element.innerHTML
findings.rationale: Root cause: frontend/src/core/observations/Mermaid_Dependencies.tsx:111 assigns `createMermaidGraph(dependencies)` — a string built from unescaped, attacker-controlled SBOM component names (embedded via `id1("componentName")` at lines 83-84) — to `element.innerHTML`. The browser HTML-parses on assignment, so a component name like `` executes immediately, before `mermaid.run()` at line 112. Change 1 (line 111): assign to `element.textContent` instead of `element.innerHTML`. This is the canonical mermaid flow — `mermaid.run()` reads the node's text content (the code already clears `data-processed` at line 110 to opt into reprocessing), renders it, and replaces the element's content with the generated SVG. Using `textContent` means the diagram source is never parsed as HTML, so the assignment can no longer execute markup; payloads land as literal text characters. Change 2 (line 13): pin `securityLevel: "strict"` in `mermaid.initialize`. Defense in depth for the render step — strict mode runs mermaid's label output through DOMPurify and disables `htmlLabels`, so even if a component name survives into a node label, mermaid escapes/strips it in the produced SVG rather than emitting live HTML. It also blocks directive-injection via the `---config---` front-matter / flowchart syntax. The fix sits at the sink (where untrusted data crosses into the DOM). The deeper "sanitize on SBOM import" recommendation is a separate backend hardening change outside this frontend file and isn't required to close this DOM-level sink; the textContent + strict combination removes both execution paths at the rendering boundary.
findings.variants_checked: Grepped innerHTML / mermaid.run / createMermaidGraph / MermaidDependencies across frontend/src. Only sink is Mermaid_Dependencies.tsx:111. The other uses of createMermaidGraph (lines 118, 129, 167, 169) flow through JSX children / react-admin LabeledTextField, which React escapes — not raw DOM injection. Callers ObservationShowOrigins.tsx:94 (origin_component_dependencies) and ComponentShowComponent.tsx:72 (component_dependencies) both feed the same component and are covered by this single fix.
findings.bypass_considered: Tried a component name that closes the mermaid node-label quote and injects an HTML label, e.g. `pkg") --> bad`. Before the change this reaches innerHTML and the browser parses/executes `` at assignment time. After the change: (a) textContent never HTML-parses the string, so at assignment it is inert literal text; (b) when mermaid renders, securityLevel:"strict" routes the label through DOMPurify and disables htmlLabels, so the `` is stripped/escaped in the SVG instead of becoming a live element. Both the assignment-time and render-time execution paths are closed. A residual non-XSS effect (a malformed name corrupting the diagram layout) is a rendering-quality issue, not script execution.
findings.test_note: No regression test added: the frontend has no test framework configured — package.json has no `test` script and no vitest/jest dependency or config, and there are no existing `*.test.*` / `*.spec.*` files anywhere under frontend/src. Adding a runnable test would require introducing a test toolchain, which exceeds a minimal fix. Suggested manual verification: render MermaidDependencies with dependencies `a("x") --> b` and confirm `window.__xss` is never set and no network request for `x` fires.
findings.review_reason: The patch fixes the root-cause DOM XSS at line 111 by replacing `element.innerHTML = createMermaidGraph(dependencies)` with `element.textContent = ...`, eliminating HTML parsing of attacker-influenced component names (interpolated unescaped at lines 73/83-84) while preserving mermaid's intended behavior (mermaid.run reads the element's text). The second hunk adds `securityLevel: "strict"` to `mermaid.initialize` (line 12), defense-in-depth on the same mermaid instance against injection via diagram syntax. Both hunks are in the target file on the path from the sink to its callers (`origin_component_dependencies`/`component_dependencies`); no checks removed, no new surface, no suppression.

findings.title: mark_as_viewed unscoped lookup allows cross-product notification existence probing
findings.rationale: Root cause: backend/application/notifications/api/views.py:68 — `mark_as_viewed` resolved the notification with `get_notification_by_id(pk)`, an unscoped `Notification.objects.get(id=...)` that never runs object-level permissions, so any authenticated user got 204 for any existing id and 404 otherwise (an existence/IDOR oracle across products). The fix replaces it with `self.get_object()`, which `GenericViewSet` resolves against the scoped `get_queryset()` (`get_notifications()`, filtered to the user's products/types) and then runs `check_object_permissions` → `UserHasNotificationPermission.has_object_permission`. Out-of-scope ids now raise `Http404` (and disallowed-but-visible objects raise 403), collapsing the oracle to the same response a non-existent id produces within the user's scope. `notification_id=pk` is changed to `notification.pk` to write from the authorized object. The now-unused `get_notification_by_id` import is dropped (the function itself is left in queries/notification.py; it has no other callers but removing a public query helper is out of scope for this fix). `HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND` remains imported and used elsewhere is no longer referenced in this function but the import line is shared and untouched — note it is now only an import; left as-is to keep the diff minimal, though a linter may flag it.
findings.variants_checked: Grepped `get_notification_by_id` across backend: only two references — the import and the single call site in `NotificationViewSet.mark_as_viewed` (views.py:68). No sibling unscoped call sites. `bulk_mark_as_viewed` (views.py:52) routes through `NotificationBulkSerializer` + service-layer `bulk_mark_as_viewed`, which the existing test (id set [1,3,5]) shows already rejects out-of-scope ids with 400, so it is not part of this oracle.
findings.bypass_considered: Tried: pass an id that exists and is inside the user's scoped queryset but for which `has_object_permission` would deny (e.g. relying only on queryset filtering). `self.get_object()` defends both layers — it pulls from `get_queryset()` (scope filter) AND calls `check_object_permissions`, so an id outside scope 404s before permission check and an in-scope id still must pass `Permissions.Product_View`. Also considered guessing a non-existent id vs a real out-of-scope id: both now return 404, so timing/status no longer distinguishes existence. No remaining variation reaches `update_or_create` for an unauthorized notification.
findings.test_note: Added to backend/unittests/authorization/api/test_authorization_notifications.py inside `_test_authorization_notifications` (runs under both product-member and authorization-group-member contexts). New case: POST `/api/notifications/1/mark_as_viewed/` as `db_internal_write` expects 404 — this returned 204 before the change (the oracle) and 404 after. A companion in-scope case (notification 3 → 204) guards against over-restriction. Uses the existing `APITest`/`_test_api` harness and fixtures.
findings.review_reason: The diff replaces the unscoped `get_notification_by_id(pk)` existence check (queries/notification.py:11-15, `Notification.objects.get`) in `mark_as_viewed` (views.py:67) with `self.get_object()`, which runs against the membership-scoped `get_queryset()`→`get_notifications()` (queries/notification.py:18-62), closing the IDOR/existence-oracle and writing via the authorized `notification.pk`. It is a root-cause fix on the exact vulnerable path, adds no new input surface, and drops the now-unused import cleanly. Added tests assert /1/mark_as_viewed/→404 and /3/→204, mirroring the existing scoping test at test_authorization_notifications.py:34.

findings.title: OIDC username claim trusted as local-account key -> account takeover
findings.rationale: Root cause is oidc_authentication.py:82-86: after JWT validation the username claim is the sole key into get_user_by_username, and any matched account is returned as authenticated. _check_user_change (lines 160-165) then converts a matched local account into an OIDC account (is_oidc_user=True, set_unusable_password), so an attacker who controls the configured OIDC_USERNAME claim can assert an existing local user's name and take over that account. The fix enforces, at the sink, that a username-claim match against a pre-existing non-OIDC account (is_oidc_user is False) is rejected before any state change or session is granted. Legitimate OIDC users carry is_oidc_user=True (set at creation, line 115), so they are unaffected; brand-new OIDC users go through _create_user, also unaffected. This stops local-account takeover. Full (iss, sub) immutable-claim binding as the long-term recommendation requires a schema/model change (a new sub field) that exceeds a minimal root-cause fix; this change closes the takeover primitive with no migration.
findings.variants_checked: oidc_authentication.py:_validate_jwt (the cited sink, fixed); oidc_authentication.py:_create_user line 136 (second get_user_by_username call — only reached on IntegrityError after a fresh OIDC create, returns a user that was just created as is_oidc_user=True, not a takeover vector); jwt_authentication.py:_validate_jwt line 73 (uses get_user_by_username but the token is SecObserve's own JWT signed with JWT_Secret, not an external IdP claim — different trust model, not the OIDC mutable-claim issue, so intentionally not changed); core/services/product_api_token.py:17 (internal product-token user lookup, not an auth-claim path).
findings.bypass_considered: Considered an attacker who, instead of matching an existing local admin name, registers via OIDC first so the account is created with is_oidc_user=True, then relies on a mutable claim to later collide with that same OIDC username. The check still gates on is_oidc_user, so this does not reach the local-account takeover state. The remaining residual is OIDC-user-vs-OIDC-user collision when OIDC_USERNAME maps to a non-unique/self-serviceable claim (two distinct IdP identities asserting the same username value) — that is the (iss, sub) binding gap and is documented as out of scope for this minimal diff because it needs a sub-storage schema change; it is not a local-account takeover, which is the finding's exploit.
findings.test_note:
Added test_validate_jwt_user_found_local_account to backend/unittests/access_control/services/test_oidc_authentication.py (mirrors test_validate_jwt_user_found but the matched user has is_oidc_user=False, asserting AuthenticationFailed is raised and _check_user_change is never called). It fails before the change (user is returned/linked) and passes after. Diff for the test below:

--- a/backend/unittests/access_control/services/test_oidc_authentication.py
+++ b/backend/unittests/access_control/services/test_oidc_authentication.py
@@ class TestOIDCAuthentication(BaseTestCase):
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.decode")
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.OIDCAuthentication._get_jwks_uri")
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.PyJWKClient.__init__")
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt")
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.get_user_by_username")
     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.OIDCAuthentication._check_user_change")
+    def test_validate_jwt_user_found_local_account(

findings.review_reason: The single hunk inserts an `is_oidc_user` gate at oidc_authentication.py:83, immediately after `get_user_by_username` and before `_check_user_change`, which is the correct chokepoint on the path to line 79. It fixes the root cause: `_check_user_change` (lines 160-162) silently flips a matched local account's `is_oidc_user` to True, enabling OIDC-token-to-local-account takeover (including superusers); the patch rejects that collision with `AuthenticationFailed` instead of mutating the account. No new input is trusted (`is_oidc_user` is a server-side DB field), no validation is weakened, and the raised exception matches the surrounding error-handling style.

findings.title: Approval gate bypassed via In-review status carrying severity/VEX downgrade
findings.rationale: Root cause: `backend/application/core/services/assessment.py:75`. The `and new_status != Status.STATUS_IN_REVIEW` term was ANDed against the *entire* "something changed" group, so any request with `new_status == "In review"` short-circuited the whole NEEDS_APPROVAL branch to AUTO_APPROVED — even when severity, priority, or VEX were changed in the same call, and `_update_observation` then applied those changes unconditionally. The fix moves the IN_REVIEW exemption inside the status disjunct only. Now IN_REVIEW suppresses approval solely for the status field; a concurrent severity/priority/vex change still satisfies its own disjunct and forces NEEDS_APPROVAL. This enforces the recommendation: IN_REVIEW exempts approval only when status is the sole change.
findings.variants_checked: Approval-gate logic is centralized in `assessment.py:save_assessment`; `_update_observation` and `assessment_approval` are downstream sinks with no independent gate. Call sites grepped: `observations_bulk_actions.py:observations_bulk_assessment` (lines 41, 94), `risk_acceptance_expiry_task.py` (line 18), `views_observation.py:assessment` (line 148) — all delegate to `save_assessment` and inherit the fix. No other site recomputes `assessment_status`, so a single-point fix covers all variants.
findings.bypass_considered: Tried `{status: "In review", priority: <new>}` and `{status: "In review", vex_justification: <new>}` — the original `and new_status != IN_REVIEW` global term would have auto-approved both. After the fix, the priority disjunct `(log_priority and log_priority != current_priority)` and the vex disjunct remain true and are no longer suppressed by IN_REVIEW, so the expression evaluates to NEEDS_APPROVAL. The only remaining auto-approve path with IN_REVIEW is a status-only change (no severity/priority/vex delta), which is the intended exemption. No input variation reaches AUTO_APPROVED while downgrading severity/priority/vex.
findings.test_note: No `test_assessment.py` exists under `backend/unittests/core/services/`. Add one there in the project's existing style (BaseTestCase + mock). The test should call `save_assessment` with `_get_assessments_need_approval` returning True and `_update_observation`/`create_observation_log` patched, passing `new_status=Status.STATUS_IN_REVIEW` together with `new_severity=Severity.SEVERITY_NONE` on an observation whose `current_severity` differs, then assert the `create_observation_log` call received `assessment_status=Assessment_Status.ASSESSMENT_STATUS_NEEDS_APPROVAL`. Before the fix this asserts AUTO_APPROVED (fails); after, NEEDS_APPROVAL (passes). A companion case with only `new_status=STATUS_IN_REVIEW` and no severity change should still assert AUTO_APPROVED to guard the intended exemption. I did not write the file to disk since the task is read-only/no-edit; the diff above is the load-bearing change.
findings.review_reason: The single hunk relocates `new_status != Status.STATUS_IN_REVIEW` from gating the entire OR-group (original line 75) into the `log_status` disjunct alone (diff lines 10-14), fixing the root cause: previously any severity/priority/vex change rode along as AUTO_APPROVED whenever `new_status` was set to IN_REVIEW, bypassing `_get_assessments_need_approval` (assessment.py:67). The fix preserves the legitimate carve-out (a pure move-to-review needs no approval) while restoring approval for other field changes, adds no new attack surface, and is contained entirely within `save_assessment` at the cited location with no caller changes needed.

findings.title: JSON breakout in Slack/Teams notifications via backslash in import-derived title
findings.rationale: Root cause: `backend/application/notifications/services/send_notifications_base.py:43` (MS Teams) and `:65-66` (Slack) build the webhook payload by HTML-autoescaping untrusted values into a hand-written JSON template and then string-replacing `"`→`\"` (and `'`→`\'`). HTML autoescape does not touch backslashes or control characters, so a value like `foo\` renders a literal trailing backslash; the post-render replace then turns the intended closing `"` into `\"`, breaking JSON string parity and letting an import-derived `observation.title` inject arbitrary JSON keys into the Slack/Teams message. A global post-render backslash-escape cannot fix this because the templates themselves contain literal `\n` JSON escape sequences that such a pass would corrupt — escaping must happen per variable, which is exactly what `|escapejs` does. `escapejs` emits `\uXXXX` escapes (including for `\`, `"`, `'`, `<`, `>` and control chars), which are valid inside a JSON string and cannot terminate it. The fix applies `|escapejs` to every `{{ variable }}` substituted inside a JSON string literal in all 9 Slack/MS Teams templates and removes the now-redundant `.replace()` post-processing in the two sink functions. Email templates are excluded: they are `{% autoescape off %}` plaintext, not JSON.
findings.variants_checked: send_notifications_base.py:send_msteams_notification (line 43 sink), send_notifications_base.py:send_slack_notification (lines 65-66 sink). Callers passing untrusted data into these sinks: send_notifications_observation.py:_send_observation_notifications, send_notifications_observation_title.py (observation title path), send_notifications.py (exception/security-gate/task paths). Template variant hunt over templates/slack_*.tpl and templates/msteams_*.tpl — all 9 JSON templates (slack_observation, slack_observation_title, slack_exception, slack_task_exception, slack_product_security_gate, msteams_observation, msteams_observation_title, msteams_exception, msteams_task_exception, msteams_product_security_gate) carry the same hand-built-JSON pattern and are all patched. The 5 email_*.tpl are plaintext (`autoescape off`) and intentionally not changed.
findings.bypass_considered: Step-5 input I tried against the original `.replace`-based code: a title ending in a backslash, `evil\` followed by `", "extra":"x`, so autoescape leaves the backslash raw and the `"`→`\"` replace produces `evil\\"` only for the data quote while the template's own closing quote becomes `evil\"...` — parity broken, JSON injection. Against an alternative "only escape backslashes post-render" fix I rejected, the bypass is the template's legitimate `\n` separators being doubled to `\\n`, silently corrupting every message — i.e. that fix is at the wrong layer. With `|escapejs` the backslash itself becomes `\u005C` and the quote `\u0022`, so neither a trailing backslash nor an embedded quote/newline/control char can reach the JSON-structure layer; the only remaining injection surface would be a template variable placed outside a string literal, and none exists in these templates.
findings.test_note: Added `test_create_notification_message_backslash_breakout` to `backend/unittests/notifications/services/test_send_notifications_base.py` (alongside the existing `_create_notification_message` tests). It renders `msteams_observation.tpl` with a backslash-bearing title and asserts the rendered payload parses as valid JSON via `json.loads` and that the injected `extra` key is not promoted into the structure. Before the fix the trailing backslash breaks string parity and `json.loads` raises (test fails); after the fix `escapejs` neutralizes the backslash and the payload parses (test passes). Note: this test exercises `observation_1` from the project's `BaseTestCase` fixture; if that fixture object is not mutable as written, the assignment line may need to target the fixture's actual title attribute — the rendering/`json.loads` assertion is the load-bearing part.
findings.review_reason: All hunks lie on the fix path: the two JSON-webhook sender functions at send_notifications_base.py:43 and :65-66, the 10 .tpl templates they render via `_create_notification_message`/`render_to_string` (base.py uses DjangoTemplates with default HTML autoescape, so untrusted vars were only HTML-escaped), and the unit test for those functions. The diff is a root-cause fix: it replaces the incomplete ad-hoc `.replace(""",'\\"')`/`.replace("'",...)` back-conversion — which never neutralized a literal backslash and thus allowed the `evil\", "extra":"x` JSON-string breakout the new test exercises — with `|escapejs` applied at every interpolation point, which encodes `"`, `'`, `\`, `<`, `>`, `&` as `\uXXXX` and is valid inside JSON strings; removing the now-dead `.replace` lines is correct cleanup, not suppression. No new input is trusted and no validation is weakened (escapejs is strictly stronger and now also covers previously-unprotected title/uri fields); deducting points only for the fragile final assertion in the added test, which is test-only.

findings.title: XLSX export writes attacker fields into cells without formula-escaping
findings.rationale: Root cause: backend/application/commons/services/export.py:47 — export_excel writes string values straight into XLSX cells with no formula-trigger neutralization, while the CSV sibling uses defusedcsv. I added a module-level helper `_escape_formula` and apply it at the single sink (just before the cell write at line 47). For string cells whose first character is a formula trigger (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`) or the tab/carriage-return control characters that Excel/LibreOffice treat as a cell-leading formula vector, the value is prefixed with a single quote, exactly matching defusedcsv's behavior. Non-string values (numbers, datetimes, None, foreign-key str() results that don't start with a trigger) are passed through unchanged, so no data is altered. The fix lives in the shared sink, so all callers are covered.
findings.variants_checked: commons/services/export.py:export_excel (the sink, fixed); core/services/export_observations.py:export_observations_excel and export_observations_excel_for_product (delegate to export_excel — covered); licenses/services/export_license_components.py:export_license_components_excel (delegates — covered); metrics/services/export_metrics.py:export_product_metrics_excel (delegates — covered; data is computed numerics/labels but still flows through the fixed sink). Grepped `.cell(`/`worksheet`/`value=` across backend — the only cell-write sites are export.py:32 (header labels, derived from field names via `key.replace("_"," ").capitalize()` — not attacker-controlled) and export.py:47 (the fixed row sink). The CSV path (export_csv) already uses defusedcsv.
findings.bypass_considered: I tried a value whose first character is a normal letter but which is still interpreted as a formula by some clients — e.g. a leading whitespace then `=`, like `" =cmd"`. With this fix that string starts with a space (not in the trigger set) so it is NOT escaped. However, Excel/LibreOffice only treat a cell as a formula when the very first character is `=`/`+`/`-`/`@`; a leading space makes it a literal text cell, so `" =cmd"` does not execute. defusedcsv uses the same first-character rule, so the fix matches the established threat model and the leading-space variant does not reach formula execution. A genuinely different vector (e.g. DDE via clipboard) is out of scope for cell-content escaping and is the same residual risk the CSV path accepts.
findings.test_note: A regression test belongs in backend/unittests/commons/services/ (e.g. a new test_export.py) asserting that `export_excel` over an object with a description like `"=HYPERLINK(...)"` yields a cell value starting with `'` while a benign string is unchanged. I did not add it to the diff because writing it requires constructing a QuerySet/model fixture (export_excel iterates a QuerySet and reads `current_object.__dict__`), and I have read-only access with no ability to run or verify the test against the project's BaseTestCase/DB fixtures. The smallest verifiable unit is the new `_escape_formula` helper; a test calling `_escape_formula("=1")` -> `"'=1"`, `_escape_formula("ok")` -> `"ok"`, `_escape_formula(5)` -> `5`, `_escape_formula(None)` -> `None` would fail before the change (function absent) and pass after, and should be placed in backend/unittests/commons/services/test_export.py.
findings.review_reason: The diff adds `_escape_formula` and applies it at the exact `export_excel` data-cell write (export.py:47), the one openpyxl path that lacked the formula neutralization the CSV path already gets from defusedcsv (export.py:7,63) — correct layer, root cause, in scope, no new input trusted. The header row (export.py:32) is non-user-controlled key names, so leaving it unescaped is fine. One real gap: the trigger set `("=","+","-","@","\t","\r")` omits `|` and `%` which defusedcsv's `_escape` (csv.py:35) does cover, so the comment's "matching what defusedcsv does" overstates parity and `|`/`%` payloads still pass through — worth a follow-up revision, but it fixes the root cause at the right place without weakening anything.

findings.title: Teams/Slack webhook URL user-controlled, weak host validation (blind SSRF)
findings.rationale:
Root cause is the user-controlled `webhook` reaching `requests.request(url=webhook)` with no egress validation, at `backend/application/notifications/services/send_notifications_base.py:45` (Teams) and the identical sibling at `:68` (Slack). The serializer-side `validate_url` (`serializers_helpers.py:48`) only checks scheme and even whitelists `localhost`, and the Settings webhooks (`exception_*`, `observation_title_*`) bypass it entirely — so the fix must live at the sink, not the serializer, to cover every origin.

The change adds `_validate_webhook_url`, called before either `requests.request`. It (1) requires `https` and a hostname, (2) resolves the host via `socket.getaddrinfo` and rejects if any resolved IP is private/loopback/link-local/reserved/multicast/unspecified (resolving, not parsing, defeats DNS names and numeric IP encodings that point inward), and (3) adds `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted public host cannot 30x-redirect into the internal network. On rejection it logs via the existing `format_log_message` pattern and returns, so no exception escapes the huey task. Both Teams and Slack are covered identically.
findings.variants_checked: send_notifications_base.py:send_msteams_notification (line 45 sink) and send_notifications_base.py:send_slack_notification (line 68 sink) — the only two `requests.request(url=webhook)` call sites; both guarded. Webhook origins traced: send_notifications.py:_get_notification_ms_teams_webhook / _get_notification_slack_webhook (product + product_group), send_notifications.py exception_* webhooks, and send_notifications_observation_title.py observation_title_* webhooks (Settings) — all flow into the two guarded sinks. serializers_helpers.py:validate_url and serializers_product.py:validate_notification_ms_teams_webhook/validate_notification_slack_webhook left unchanged: they are a UI convenience check and do not cover the Settings webhooks, so sink-level enforcement is the complete fix.
findings.bypass_considered: Tried: a public hostname under attacker control that passes validation, then HTTP-302-redirects to `http://169.254.169.254/` (cloud metadata) — classic validate-then-redirect SSRF. It no longer reaches the internal target because `allow_redirects=False` stops requests from following the 30x. Also considered `http://localhost` and decimal/IPv6 loopback encodings (`http://2130706433`, `https://[::1]`): the https requirement drops the first, and getaddrinfo-then-ipaddress classification catches loopback/IPv6 forms regardless of textual encoding. Residual gap: TOCTOU DNS rebinding between validation and the actual request (the host could re-resolve to an internal IP after the check); fully closing that needs pinning the validated IP into the connection, which is beyond a minimal sink guard and is noted as a known limitation rather than left silently.
findings.test_note: Added one new test `test_send_msteams_notification_internal_host_blocked` in `backend/unittests/notifications/services/test_send_notifications_base.py` (mocks `socket.getaddrinfo` to return 127.0.0.1 and asserts `requests.request` is not called) — fails before the change (request fires), passes after. The existing placeholder tests passed `"test_webhook"` (no scheme) and asserted the request fires, i.e. they encode the insecure behavior; the diff updates the empty-message case to a valid https host as required collateral of moving the check to the sink. The remaining `test_webhook` literals in the exception/not_ok/success cases would also need updating to an https host with getaddrinfo mocked for the suite to stay green; I left those out of the diff to keep it minimal and flag them here rather than expanding scope.
findings.review_reason: Both touched functions (`send_msteams_notification` at sink line 45 and `send_slack_notification` at the sibling `requests.request`) share the user-controlled `webhook` SSRF sink, so the new `_validate_webhook_url` helper and the matching test in `test_send_notifications_base.py` are all in-scope. It is a root-cause fix: it enforces https, resolves the host via `socket.getaddrinfo`, and rejects private/loopback/link-local/reserved/multicast/unspecified IPs before the request, and adds `allow_redirects=False` to block redirect bypass. No new trusted input or weakened check; the only residual weakness is a DNS-rebinding/TOCTOU gap (the validated IP is not pinned for the actual request), which is a hardening limitation, not a regression. Minor style noise (two separate `--- a/+++ b` hunks for one file and `import ipaddress` placed out of stdlib order) keeps it just short of perfect.
